newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania rejects concessions by Burundi leader.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania rejects concessions by Burundi leader.

text.p: Tanzania refused on Wednesday to ease sanctions against Burundi in return for Tutsi military leader Pierre Buyoya's lifting bans on parliament and political parties.

The Tanzanian foreign ministry said Buyoya had failed to act on the most important demand by regional leaders: unconditional negotiations with all parties to the conflict both inside and outside Burundi.

It said Buyoya's concessions lacked detail and fell short of demands made at regional summits in Arusha, northern Tanzania, on June 25 and June 31 for talks on power-sharing with the Hutu National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).

"The announcement by Major Pierre Buyoya is therefore far from satisfactory because the return to legality and constitutionality of Burundi cannot be free and complete when the security of parliamentarians and party officials is predicated at the mercy of the army which is the de facto government," the statement said.
"Under the circumstances, the government of Tanzania is still waiting for concrete steps to be taken by the Buyoya regime before it can address itself to the issue of relaxing sanctions," it added.

It said only after the unconditional fulfillment of all three conditions stipulated at the Arusha summits would talks chaired by former president Julius Nyerere in the Lake Victoria town of Mwanza be reconvened. Power-sharing is key to them.
Buyoya, who seized power from Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya in a July 25 coup by the Tutsi-dominated army, last Friday lifted bans on political parties and parliament.
But he says he cannot open unconditional negotiations with Hutu rebels and demands they first lay down their weapons.
Fears are widespread that Burundi might go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda, where up to a million people were killed in genocide and three months of civil war in 1994.
Buyoya's leadership, which expects to rule for a three -year transitional period, said on Sunday it would stick to its programme even if it did not win an immediate end to sanctions.
